title: America's F-47 May Fly Without Its Intended Engine, Echoing India's AMCA Challenge
excerpt: Supply chain delays have pushed the F-47's next-generation engine back by two years, forcing the Pentagon to consider interim powerplants — a compromise India's own stealth fighter program knows well.
body:
• The U.S. Air Force's F-47 sixth-generation fighter may enter service without its intended NGAP adaptive engine due to a two-year supply chain delay
  • Budget documents show NGAP funding cut by $100 million in 2026, from $439.9 million to $330.3 million
  • India's AMCA program faces a parallel engine gap — the Mk-1 will use American GE F414 engines while a next-gen powerplant is co-developed with France's Safran
  • Turkey's KAAN and Russia's Su-57 have also resorted to interim engines, making it a global pattern in advanced fighter development

Pentagon's Engine Dilemma

The Boeing F-47, the centerpiece of America's Next Generation Air Dominance (NGAD) program, faces a critical propulsion shortfall. The Next-Generation Adaptive Propulsion (NGAP) engine — designed to give the sixth-generation fighter variable-cycle capabilities for both fuel-efficient cruising and high-thrust combat — has been delayed by two years, according to Defense Express, citing a U.S. Air Force statement to Breaking Defense.

The NGAP prototype, originally expected in late 2027, is now projected for the second quarter of 2030. Engine manufacturer General Electric maintains that development remains on schedule and could be accelerated, though budget figures complicate that claim.

"In 2026, the NGAP program will receive $330.3 million, down from $439.9 million in 2025 — a significant $100 million reduction."

— Defense Express analysis of Pentagon budget documents

The Air Force attributes the funding cut to a natural transition from design to system refinement. But the reduction, combined with recent cancellations of classified programs like the E-7 Wedgetail and cuts to the Navy's F/A-XX, suggests broader fiscal pressures on next-generation defense programs.

The Fallback: Interim Engines

With the F-47's first flight still targeted within the next four years, the timeline now clashes with engine availability. One option is to equip early production aircraft with existing engines — a path already trodden by other nations' advanced fighter programs.

Russia's Su-57 has been flying with older AL-41 engines rather than its intended Saturn Izdeliye 30 powerplant. Turkey's KAAN fifth-generation fighter made its maiden flight in February 2024 powered by American F110 engines, with a domestic engine years away from completion.

This stopgap approach carries real penalties: integration risks, performance compromises, and costly future upgrades, particularly if the airframe is optimized around the NGAP's variable-cycle architecture.

India's Parallel Struggle

India's Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) faces a strikingly similar predicament. The ₹15,000 crore ($1.70 billion) program, led by DRDO's Aeronautical Development Agency, will produce two variants. The AMCA Mk-1 will use American GE F414 engines — the same powerplant whose deliveries for the Tejas Mk1A ran two years late, according to SPS Aviation.

The more advanced AMCA Mk-2 will require a 120-kilonewton engine being co-developed by India's Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE) and France's Safran under a deal worth an estimated ₹61,000 crore ($6.4 billion). That engine, incorporating adaptive cycle technology, remains a decade away from completion.

Seven Indian companies and consortia submitted proposals in September 2025 to build the AMCA airframe, including HAL, Larsen & Toubro, Adani Defence, and Tata Advanced Systems. Serial production is projected to begin by 2035, but the engine timeline remains the program's critical bottleneck.

A Global Pattern

The engine gap is becoming a defining challenge of next-generation fighter development worldwide. Adaptive cycle engines — capable of adjusting bypass ratios in flight to balance range and power — represent a generational leap in propulsion technology. No nation has yet fielded one.

China is working on adaptive cycle engines for future fighters, having already begun equipping its J-20 stealth fighter with domestically produced WS-15 engines. The UK-Italy-Japan GCAP (Tempest) program targets a 2030 first flight, adding competitive pressure.

For the Indian diaspora watching these developments, the AMCA engine challenge carries particular weight. India's ability to co-develop a world-class fighter engine with Safran would mark a transformational step in its aerospace capabilities — but the F-47's troubles show that even the world's largest defense spender struggles with the same technological frontier.
nri_angle: India's AMCA engine co-development with Safran mirrors the F-47's propulsion challenges, underscoring the difficulty of achieving aerospace self-reliance.
